props.title: Love & Pop
props.initialSlug: A love story like no other.

sections.content: **Love & Pop (1998)** (1998) marks Hideaki Anno's radical departure from animation into live-action, using digital cameras to create a dizzying exploration of teenage enjo-kōsai (compensated dating) in Tokyo. Shot with over 200 miniature digital cameras in unconventional angles, the film shares DNA with Anno's psychological masterpiece **Neon Genesis Evangelion** (1995), particularly in its unflinching examination of youth alienation. The experimental cinematography - with cameras mounted on everything from drinking glasses to moving trains - creates a voyeuristic, disorienting effect that mirrors its protagonist's fractured reality.

sections.content: Anno's transition to digital filmmaking in 1998 preceded the Japanese "digital revolution" that would birth works like All About Lily Chou-Chou (2001) and **Nobody Knows** (2004). The intimate, handheld aesthetic allowed filmmakers to capture youth culture with unprecedented immediacy. **Love & Pop** employs these techniques not just as budget necessity but as artistic statement - the consumer-grade cameras mirror the commodification of its teenage protagonists.

The film's influence extends beyond Japanese cinema. Its exploration of technology-mediated adolescence presages works like **thirteen** (2003) and **Spring Breakers** (2012). The fragmented visual style, achieved through multiple small cameras and extreme angles, established a vocabulary for depicting disaffected youth that would influence filmmakers like Harmony Korine and Larry Clark. sections.content: The late 1990s saw Japanese cinema grappling with changing youth culture through new digital tools. While **Love & Pop** used technology to examine teenage exploitation, films like **Battle Royale** (2000) and Suicide Club (2001) approached similar themes through genre frameworks. Anno's documentary-like approach, however, brought an uncomfortable intimacy to the subject matter that many subsequent films would emulate.
